title: Motion to Intervene and Protest of Lisa Melton re the Grid-Reliability and Capacity Implications of Large-Load Interconnection and Associated Energy Infrastructure in Box Elder County, Utah under RM26-4.

documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA BEFORE THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



) In the Matter of:           ) Large Load Interconnection Rulemaking     ) Docket No.
RM26-4-000 ) Ruby Pipeline, L.L.C.            ) Docket No. RP26-358-000 )



MOTION TO INTERVENE AND PROTEST



Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (FERC or
Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211 and 385.214, the
undersigned Intervenor hereby submits this Motion to Intervene and Protest.



RE: Intervention Regarding the Grid-Reliability and Capacity Implications of Large-Load
Interconnection and Associated Energy Infrastructure, Box Elder County, Utah.



To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission:



The undersigned submits this Motion as a directly affected stakeholder concerned with the
technical, physical, and economic stability of the Western Interconnection. Intervenor's
interest rests on the grid-reliability consequences of introducing very large, concentrated
loads onto the regional energy system — consequences squarely within the scope of the
Commission's Large Load Interconnection Rulemaking and its review of associated
interstate pipeline interconnections. That interest places Intervenor within the community
of persons affected by the outcome of these dockets.



The proposed 40,000-acre Stratos data center project requires a direct infrastructure
interconnection to the interstate Ruby Pipeline, under the jurisdiction of this Commission,
and a major New Source Review (NSR) Air Permit, under the jurisdiction of the U.S.
Environmental Protection Agency, to burn natural gas for an on-site 9-gigawatt power
generation facility.

1. Establishment of a Clear Federal Nexus and "But For" Causality
 The Stratos project cannot proceed without multiple, indispensable federal actions:



FERC Jurisdiction. The physical tap, delivery interconnection, and negotiated rate
allocations on the interstate Ruby Pipeline (Docket No. RP26-358-000) require the direct
regulatory approval of this Commission.



EPA Jurisdiction. The carbon and particulate emissions from the proposed 9-GW gas plant
require federal Title V and Clean Air Act authorizations.



The federal nexus here is direct and dispositive. But for this Commission's approval of the
Ruby Pipeline interconnection and associated rate authorizations in Docket No. RP26-358-
000, the proposed 9-gigawatt gas generation facility has no fuel supply. Without fuel
delivery, the generation facility cannot be built or operated. And without that generation
facility, the 9-gigawatt load cannot be energized and the associated capacity and reliability
impacts on the Western Interconnection cannot occur.



The Commission's approval of the pipeline interconnection is therefore the indispensable
causal predicate for the entire chain of capacity and systemic impacts that follow. Federal
action is not one factor among many; it is the gate through which every downstream effect
must pass. That is precisely why the Commission's review of these interconnections must
be rigorous, and must occur before — not after — the interconnection and rate
authorizations are granted.

2. Grid Capacity and Reliability Divergence

Introducing a sudden 9-gigawatt footprint imposes large and potentially destabilizing
capacity demands on the Western Interconnection. A load of this magnitude, concentrated
at a single site and dependent on dedicated on-site fossil generation, raises reliability
questions that the Commission should not resolve by default approval:



Capacity strain. A 9-GW addition is not a marginal increment. It is a step change in
regional demand that affects reserve margins, congestion, and the planning assumptions
underlying the interconnection.
 Concentration risk. A single 40,000-acre facility dependent on a single pipeline
interconnection and dedicated on-site generation concentrates reliability risk in a way that
distributed load does not.



Lock-in. Approving a fossil-fuel-dependent interconnection of this scale commits the
regional system to a long-lived capacity and emissions profile that is difficult to reverse
once built.



Within the scope of the Large Load Interconnection Rulemaking (Docket No. RM26-4-000),
the Commission should expressly evaluate whether loads of this magnitude can be
reduced, managed, or avoided through advanced load-management and grid-
synchronization approaches generally — including demand-side flexibility, load-shaping
requirements, ride-through and interconnection-conditioning standards, and comparable
measures — rather than approving large fossil-fuel-reliant interconnections by default in a
manner that locks in irreversible systemic harm. Intervenor does not ask the Commission
to adopt any particular proprietary methodology; Intervenor asks that the rulemaking
require such alternatives to be evaluated as part of the record before large-load
interconnections of this scale are authorized.

3. Environmental Implications Within the Commission's Review

The scale of this project also raises environmental concerns relevant to the federal
authorizations at issue:



Air quality and climate footprint. Burning natural gas to generate 9 gigawatts of power
threatens a substantial increase in regional carbon and particulate emissions.



Hydrological strain. Converting vast acreage of open rangeland into an impervious
industrial campus permanently alters natural drainage basins, posing water-table and
ecological threats to the nearby Great Salt Lake ecosystem — a system already the subject
of significant regional environmental concern.
 These effects are properly considered as part of the federal review triggered by the
interconnection and air authorizations, and weigh in favor of rigorous evaluation rather than
default approval.

4. MIDA Cannot Preempt Federal Statutory Obligations

State-level actions taken by Utah's Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA) and
the Box Elder County Commission are the subject of active constitutional litigation in
Utah's Third District Court (Alliance for a Better Utah v. MIDA). That litigation directly
challenges MIDA's authority to strip local citizens of their legislative and referendum rights.



The Commission must not treat any MIDA determination as a substitute for, or a waiver of,
rigorous federal review. The principle is absolute: a state economic-development authority
has no power to contract away, delegate around, or immunize federal agencies from their
independent statutory obligations under federal environmental and energy law. Federal
duties arise under federal law and bind federal agencies directly; they cannot be
extinguished, narrowed, or satisfied by state or local zoning instruments, development
agreements, or authority determinations of any kind.



That conclusion is only reinforced by the posture of the state proceedings. The MIDA
overrides are contested, non-final, and the subject of pending constitutional challenge. A
federal agency may not rest a decision to forgo or curtail its review on a state authorization
that is legally disputed and not yet final. To defer to MIDA under these circumstances would
be to allow a contested, non-final state instrument to override a binding federal mandate.

5. Formal Requests

As an affected stakeholder in the reliability of the Western Interconnection, Intervenor
respectfully requests that the Commission:



Grant intervention. Grant Intervenor official party status in Docket Nos. RM26-4-000 and
RP26-358-000.



Require evaluation of alternatives. Within the Large Load Interconnection Rulemaking,
require that advanced load-management and grid-synchronization alternatives be
 evaluated as part of the record before large-scale, fossil-fuel-reliant pipeline
interconnections of this magnitude are authorized.



Conduct rigorous review. Decline to treat any state-level MIDA determination as a
substitute for the Commission's independent federal review of the Ruby Pipeline
interconnection and associated authorizations.



Respectfully submitted,



/s/ L.M. Marlowe



L.M. Marlowe lm.marlowe@pm.me
